372.title: Ashvala and the fire within
372.hook: the king's own priest asks how a ritual can free anyone from death, and Yajnavalkya shows him the fire is inside him too
372.tomorrow: when a person dies, what doesn't leave them?
372.howItsDone: Vedic fire rituals, with their four kinds of priests, are still performed in parts of India, and many Hindu homes keep a smaller fire offering, the havan or homa, for occasions like housewarmings and weddings; Vedanta teachers read passages like this as showing the inner meaning of the rite.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thousand cows with gold on their horns, and Yajnavalkya's answer: we bow to the wisest, we just want the cows. Your line was wisdom isn't claimed; it's questioned.
screen: `WISDOM ISN'T CLAIMED; IT'S QUESTIONED.`

segments.voice: The first challenger is a professional. Ashvala is King Janaka's hotri, the priest whose job at the great fire sacrifice is to recite the hymns of the Rig Veda. He has spent his life inside the ritual: the right verse, the right moment, the right pitch. So he doesn't ask about the meaning of life. He asks about his own job. You think you're the wisest? Fine. Explain to me how what I do actually works.
screen: `THE FIRST CHALLENGER.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PRIEST.` → `EXPLAIN MY OWN JOB TO ME.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, Ashvala says, everything here is caught by death. By what does the one who offers the sacrifice get free of death? By the hotri priest, Yajnavalkya answers, by fire, by speech. Speech is the hotri of the sacrifice. Speech is this fire. That is freedom; that is freedom beyond. Ashvala presses: caught by day and night? By the priest who handles the offerings, by the eye, by the sun. By the waxing and waning moon? By the priest who sings, by breath, by wind. And the sky has no stairs. How does the sacrificer climb to heaven? By the priest who oversees, by the mind, by the moon. See the pattern. Each of the four priests turns out to be a part of the person, speech, eye, breath, mind, and each of those a power of the cosmos, fire, sun, wind, moon. Yajnavalkya doesn't tell Ashvala the ritual is useless. He shows him what it's a picture of. Ashvala's technical questions get answers too, and he falls silent. Many teachers see this as one of the great moves of the Upanishads: the yajna, the fire offering, carried inward. Hindu thinkers weigh it differently. The Mimamsa school held that the rites themselves are the heart of the Veda; Vedanta teachers read passages like this as the rites pointing past themselves. Both kept the fire. So when a family pours ghee into a havan fire today, on this reading the offering happens in two places at once: in the flames, and in the people saying the words.
screen: `CAUGHT BY DEATH: HOW TO GET FREE?` · `THE PRIEST IS SPEECH; SPEECH IS FIRE.` · `FOUR PRIESTS, FOUR FACULTIES, FOUR POWERS.` · `THE FIRE RITE, CARRIED INWARD.` · then, large: `THE FIRE IS IN YOU TOO.`

segments.voice: If your home has a diya or a puja shelf, light the lamp, or just picture one; any light will do. Offer it your speech first, the words forming in your mind, like ghee into a flame. Then let your resting eyes be the sun, the breath coming and going the wind, and the mind watching all of it the moon. Nothing to perform: you're the whole offering, sitting still.

373.title: Take my hand: the whispered word was karma
373.hook: asked what's left of a person after death, Yajnavalkya takes his questioner's hand, walks him out, and talks about karma
373.carry: karma: you become what you do
373.tomorrow: a spirit told him where the lost kings went. does Yajnavalkya know?
373.howItsDone: Hindus remember the dead by name in shraddha rites, offering food and water to ancestors named in a family line; teachers of the Upanishads point to Artabhaga's dialogue as an early statement of karma.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashvala asked how a ritual frees anyone from death, and each priest turned out to be a part of the person. Your line was the fire rite points within.
screen: `THE FIRE RITE POINTS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: The second challenger is Artabhaga, and his last question is one people still ask. When a person dies, he says, their speech goes into fire, their breath into the wind, their eye into the sun, their mind into the moon, their body into the earth, their hair into the plants and trees, their blood into the waters. Then where is that person? And this time, Yajnavalkya won't answer in front of the crowd. Artabhaga, my friend, he says. Take my hand. This is for the two of us alone.
screen: `EVERYTHING GOES BACK.` → `THEN WHERE IS THAT PERSON?` → `TAKE MY HAND.`

segments.voice: Artabhaga's questions start dry. How many graspers are there, and how many over-graspers? Eight, Yajnavalkya says. The tongue grasps, and taste grasps it back. The eye grasps, and form grabs the eye. Everything we take hold of takes hold of us. When a person dies, what does not leave them? The name, Yajnavalkya says. The name is endless. Then the last question, where is the person when everything has gone back, and the hand, and the walk out of the room. The text tells us only this about their private talk. What they talked about was karma. What they praised was karma. A person becomes good by good action, and bad by bad action. And Artabhaga fell silent. Karma means action, the thing you do, and it had been a word of the ritual: the rite done right. Here two people step outside and talk about it as the thread of a life, carried past death. Some readers hear in it an early statement of the teaching Hindus still live by: you become what you do. Not luck, not cosmic revenge. Each action shapes the one who does it, and the shaping goes on. Why whisper it? The text doesn't say. Perhaps it was too serious for a contest. So when a classroom laughs that karma got someone, a Hindu teacher might gently turn it around: karma is less about what happens to them, and more about what your own actions are making of you.

segments.voice: Hindu families say their ancestors' names at shraddha, the rite for the dead. Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew or only heard of, and say their name silently. Notice it still brings a face, a voice, a way of doing things. Then let one thing they did come to mind, good or ordinary, and hold the name and the action together.

374.title: Where the lost kings went
374.hook: the third challenger brings a question he got from a spirit, and Yajnavalkya answers with the wind: each single thing, and everything together
374.carry: your breath is the world's breath
374.tomorrow: if the self is real, why can't anyone point to it?
374.howItsDone: Vayu, the wind, is honored in Hindu tradition as a deity and as the cosmic breath, and breath, prana, is at the center of practices like pranayama; Yajnavalkya's answer to Bhujyu is read as praise of wind as both the individual and the whole.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Artabhaga asked what doesn't leave a person at death, and in private, the answer was karma. Your line was karma: you become what you do.
screen: `KARMA: YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: The third challenger opens with a ghost story. When I was a student, says Bhujyu, we wandered to a house in the land of the Madras. The householder's daughter was possessed by a spirit, a gandharva. We asked it who it was, and it told us its name. Then we asked it about the ends of the world, and where the Parikshitas went. So, Yajnavalkya, I'm asking you: where did the Parikshitas go? It's a trap with the answer already in his pocket. He heard it from a spirit. Let's see if this man knows it too.
screen: `A SPIRIT IN A STUDENT'S STORY.` → `IT KNEW THE ENDS OF THE WORLD.` → `WHERE DID THE PARIKSHITAS GO?`

segments.voice: Who were the Parikshitas? The family of King Parikshit, remembered as great performers of the horse sacrifice, the one that opened this Upanishad two weeks ago. The Mahabharata tells of a Parikshit too, Arjuna's grandson; the Upanishad doesn't explain, it assumes its listeners know. Yajnavalkya answers without a pause. The spirit told you, surely, they went where those who perform the horse sacrifice go. And where is that? Then he gives a map. This world is as wide as thirty-two days of the sun's chariot. The earth surrounds it, twice as wide. The ocean surrounds the earth, twice as wide again. And between them is a gap as thin as the edge of a razor, or the wing of a fly. Through that gap, Indra, as a bird, handed the Parikshitas to the wind, and the wind carried them on. Then the key line: so wind is each single thing, and wind is everything together. Whoever knows this escapes dying again. And Bhujyu falls silent. Here's the teaching under the riddle. Across this Upanishad, breath in the body and wind in the world are paired as one power, and Hindus call the life-breath prana. Twelve days ago, breath was the one singer the demons couldn't pierce. Here, at the scale of the universe, it carries a person beyond the world. That's why breath sits near the heart of Hindu practice, from pranayama to a mantra said on the out-breath: the most personal thing you have is also the thing you share with everything.
screen: `THE FAMILY OF KING PARIKSHIT.` · `A GAP THIN AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `WIND: EACH THING, AND ALL TOGETHER.` · `PRANA: THE LIFE-BREATH.` · then, large: `YOUR BREATH IS THE WORLD'S BREATH.`

segments.voice: Hindus call this prana. Notice the tiny gap at the top of each in-breath, before the out-breath begins, thinner than a fly's wing; don't hold it, just notice it each time. Then notice that the air moving through you is the same air moving through the trees outside, and the city, and the sea. Each breath yours; all breath shared.
Vayu, wind. Yajnavalkya's answer: through a gap as thin as a razor's edge, carried by vayu, each single thing and everything together.
screen: `VAYU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Take this with you: your breath is the world's breath. Tomorrow, a practical man who wants to be shown. Until then.

segments.voice: A man starving in a famine eats leftover beans from an elephant driver to stay alive. Then the driver offers him water, and he turns it down: water, he says, I can find anywhere. That's Ushasti Chakrayana, in the Chandogya we read last month. Some readers take him to be today's challenger, Ushasta Chakrayana. Whoever he is, he's practical. He doesn't want theory. He wants to be shown. Point to it, he says, the way you'd point to a cow.
screen: `A MAN WHO SURVIVED ON LEFTOVER BEANS.` → `NO THEORY.` → `POINT TO IT.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, he says, explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, not secondhand: the self that is within everything. That is your self, Yajnavalkya answers, within everything. Which one? The one that breathes in with your in-breath and out with your out-breath. That is your self, within all. Ushasta isn't having it. You've explained it the way someone says, that's a cow, that's a horse. I asked for the direct one. And here Yajnavalkya gives the answer this day is named for: na drishter drashtaram pashyeh. You cannot see the seer of seeing. You cannot hear the hearer of hearing. You cannot think the thinker of thinking. You cannot know the knower of knowing. That is your self, within all. Everything else is sorrow. And Ushasta falls silent. This is the atman, the self, as the Upanishads teach it. Everything you can point to is something seen. The self isn't something seen. It's what's doing the seeing. Your eye sees the whole room and never once sees itself. For Yajnavalkya, that doesn't make the self far away. It makes it nearer than anything you could point to. And it changes an ordinary day. We look at faces, screens, our own reflection, and quietly ask which of them is me. The Upanishad's answer: none of them. You're the one looking.
screen: `SHOW ME THE SELF WITHIN ALL.` · `NOT LIKE POINTING AT A COW.` · `YOU CANNOT SEE THE SEER OF SEEING.` · `ATMAN: THE ONE LOOKING.` · then, large: `THE SEER, NEVER THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Hindu teachers call this self-inquiry. With your eyes open and soft, notice what you see, then gently try to turn around and find the one who's seeing; you won't find it as a thing. Close your eyes and do the same with sounds: hear, and then look for the hearer. Don't strain; rest in not finding it, and in the seeing still going on.
Ushasta. The man who wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard about the drashta, the seer, who can never be seen, because it is the one looking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ushasta wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard: you cannot see the self is the seer, never the seen of seeing. Your line was the self is the seer, never the seen.

segments.voice: Here's something odd about this debate. The next man to stand up, Kahola, asks exactly the same question Ushasta just asked, word for word: explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, the self within all. You'd expect Yajnavalkya to say: I just answered that. He doesn't. He answers again, from a completely different side. Yesterday the self was the seer you can't see. Today it's what's left when hunger, grief and death have nothing to hold on to.
screen: `THE SAME QUESTION, WORD FOR WORD.` → `A DIFFERENT ANSWER.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: That is your self, within all, Yajnavalkya says. Which one? The one beyond hunger and thirst, beyond grief and confusion, beyond old age and death. Three pairs. Hunger and thirst belong to the body. Grief and confusion belong to the mind. Old age and death belong to a life. Tradition calls these six the waves, rising and falling on the surface while the depth stays still. Then Yajnavalkya says what knowing this does to people. Knowing this self, the wise give up wanting sons, wanting wealth, wanting worlds, and live by begging. Wanting sons is really wanting wealth; wanting wealth is really wanting worlds. Both are just wanting. This is the root of sannyasa, renunciation: in Hindu life, some people take a vow, put on ochre cloth and set the wanting down, because they're looking for a self no wave can touch. Most Hindus never take that vow, and the tradition honors householders too. Then a surprising ladder. Having finished with learning, one should want to live like a child; past that, one becomes a muni, a silent sage. After all those years of memorizing the Veda, the next step is the plainness of a child. Some hear simplicity in that word, balya; Shankara reads it as the strength that knowledge gives. Either way, the scholars who came to win cows with their learning are told it's a stage, not the summit. And Kahola falls silent.

377.title: Gargi: on what is everything woven?
377.hook: a woman stands up in a courtyard full of men and asks a child's endless why, all the way up to Brahman
377.tomorrow: the father of 'you are that' stands up. what does he ask?
377.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Gargi Vachaknavi as a philosopher of the Vedic age, and her questions to Yajnavalkya are studied as part of the Brihadaranyaka's great debate.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kahola asked Ushasta's question again, and heard: the self is beyond hunger, grief and death hunger, grief and death; after learning, live like a child. Your line was the self is beyond hunger, grief and death.
screen: `THE SELF IS THE SELF IS BEYOND HUNGER, GRIEF AND DEATH HUNGER, GRIEF AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: Why is it raining? Because of the clouds. Why are there clouds? Because of the water. Why is there water? A child can keep that chain going until the grown-up says, because I said so. Now put that chain in a royal courtyard, where a woman has just stood up among the learned men of the Kuru and Panchala lands. Her name is Gargi Vachaknavi, and she's about to ask Yajnavalkya why, again and again, all the way to the top.
screen: `WHY? AND WHY THAT?` → `A WOMAN STANDS UP.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, she says, everything here is woven, back and forth, on water. On what, then, is water woven? Weaving is her picture: threads running lengthwise and crosswise, each held by another. On wind, Gargi, he says. On what is wind woven? On the worlds of the middle air. Then the worlds of the heavenly musicians. Of the sun. Of the moon. Of the stars. Of the gods. Of Indra. Of Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And on what are the worlds of Prajapati woven? On the worlds of Brahman. On what, she asks, are the worlds of Brahman woven? Here he stops her. Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. You are asking beyond a deity one shouldn't ask beyond. And Gargi falls silent. Here's the teaching. Brahman, the ultimate reality, is what everything is woven on. Every answer so far named a thing, and you can always ask what holds a thing. But what holds everything isn't one more thread in the cloth. Asking what it's woven on is like asking what's north of the North Pole. Later, in the Gita, Krishna uses the same picture: all this is strung on me, like pearls on a thread. Gargi isn't wrong to ask; she's found the edge of the question. Every Hindu parent eventually hears the small version: who made God? And who made that? This is the old answer: God isn't one more thing that needs a maker. And Gargi isn't finished. In two days, she'll stand up again, armed.
screen: `ON WHAT IS WATER WOVEN?` · `WIND, AIR, SUN, MOON, STARS, GODS.` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH, GARGI.` · `BRAHMAN: WHAT ALL IS WOVEN ON.` · then, large: `NOT ONE MORE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Feel what holds you: you on the seat, the seat on the floor, the floor on the building, the building on the earth, the earth held in space, with a breath at each step. When you reach the last one you can name, don't push for another. Rest right there, at the edge, where the answers stop and you're still held.
Gargi. The woman who asked what everything is woven on, ota and prota, warp and weft, until the answers ran out at the edge of the question.

378.title: The inner ruler
378.hook: the salt-and-banyan father of the Chandogya steps up as a challenger and hears of the one who lives inside everything, unseen
378.carry: the inner ruler lives in every being
378.tomorrow: Gargi stands up again with two questions like arrows. what are they?
378.howItsDone: The antaryamin passage is central in Sri Vaishnava theology, where God is understood as the inner ruler of all; students of other Vedanta schools study it too, and many Hindus explain the folded hands of namaste as honoring the divine within the other person.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi asked what everything is woven on, all the way to the top, until Yajnavalkya stopped her. Your line was everything is woven on Brahman.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS WOVEN ON BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: An old friend steps up. In the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni was the father who dropped salt in water and split a banyan seed for his son, and said: you are that. Now he stands up in Janaka's court as a challenger, and like Bhujyu, he brings a question from a spirit. Years ago, he says, a spirit speaking through a woman asked us: do you know the thread that strings this world, the next world and all beings together? Do you know the inner controller? Yajnavalkya, if you drive off those cows without knowing them, your head will fall off.
screen: `THE FATHER FROM THE CHANDOGYA.` → `A SPIRIT'S QUESTION.` → `THE THREAD, AND THE CONTROLLER.`

segments.voice: I know them, Yajnavalkya says. Anyone can say I know, I know, says Uddalaka. Tell us. The thread, says Yajnavalkya, is wind: like a string through beads, it holds this world and the next together. Then the inner controller, in a long chant. He who lives in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within: he is your self, the inner controller, the deathless. Then the same lines for water, fire, the sun, all beings. Then it turns inward: the breath, the eye, the mind. And the close. He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer but him. And Uddalaka falls silent. This is the antaryamin, the inner ruler, one of the great Hindu pictures of the divine: not only above the world, but inside every part of it, nearer than the thing itself knows. Ramanuja, the Vishishtadvaita teacher, took the phrase whose body the earth is and taught that the world and every soul are the body of God, who lives within them. Shankara, the Advaita teacher, read the inner controller as the one self. Either way, the person in front of you has someone living in them they may never have noticed. It's one way many Hindus explain namaste: folded hands for the one who lives inside the other.
screen: `ANYONE CAN SAY I KNOW, I KNOW.` · `THE THREAD IS WIND.` · `WHOSE BODY THE EARTH IS.` · `THE UNSEEN SEER.` · then, large: `THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath, and let the line come: lives in the breath, yet other than the breath. Then the resting eyes, then the mind with all its traffic: lives in it, yet the mind doesn't know it. If you pray, fold your hands for a moment at the end; if not, just rest them. Notice whether something steady seems to sit under each of these, watching.
Uddalaka. The teacher who asked about the thread and the antaryamin, the inner controller: the one who lives in each thing, whom the thing doesn't know, and who rules it from within.
